title: How to Get Over Being Cheated On: A Step-by-Step Guide
h1: How to Get Over Being Cheated On: A Gentle, Step-by-Step Guide
description: Learn how to get over being cheated on: handle the first days, stop blaming yourself, decide whether to stay or go and rebuild your trust and self-worth.
keyword: how to get over being cheated on
excerpt: Infidelity can shake everything you thought you knew. Here's how to get through the first days, stop blaming yourself and slowly feel like you again.
intro:
Finding out you've been cheated on can feel like the floor dropped out from under you. Memories you treasured suddenly look different. You may swing between rage, grief, numbness and an urgent need to understand why. Some moments you're fine; the next you can't breathe.

All of that is normal. Betrayal by someone you trusted is one of the most painful experiences in a relationship, and healing doesn't follow a straight line. This guide walks you through how to get over being cheated on one stage at a time: surviving the first few days, letting go of self-blame, deciding whether to stay or leave and gradually rebuilding your confidence and your ability to trust.
body:
First, know that this is not your fault

When someone cheats, the people who were betrayed very often turn the blame inward. “If I'd been more attractive, more fun, less busy…” It's an understandable reaction — blaming yourself can feel like regaining a sense of control. But it isn't accurate.

Relationships have problems, and both partners contribute to the state of a relationship. Cheating, though, is a choice one person makes instead of talking, getting help or ending things honestly. You are not responsible for someone else's decision to betray your trust.

Tip: Write this down somewhere you'll see it: “Their choice says something about them, not about my worth.” Read it whenever the self-blame starts.

Getting through the first few days

The early days after discovery are about survival, not big decisions. Focus on the basics:

  • Eat something, even if it's small. Shock can kill your appetite.
  • Try to sleep. Rest makes everything a little more manageable. If you can't sleep, at least lie down and rest your body.
  • Move your body. A walk around the block helps burn off stress hormones.
  • Take a shower or a bath. Simple sensory comfort can steady you when your mind is racing.
  • Avoid big announcements. You don't have to post, confront everyone or decide the future of your relationship today.

If you share a home or children, it may help to agree on some temporary space while you think.

Lean on your people

Betrayal is isolating. You might feel embarrassed or worried about what others will think, but you don't have to carry this alone. Reach out to one or two people you trust completely — a close friend, a sibling, a parent — and tell them what happened. You don't need them to fix anything. You need someone to sit with you in it.

Be a little selective. Choose people who will support you rather than pressure you toward a decision before you're ready.

Let yourself feel all of it

There's no correct way to feel after infidelity. Anger, sadness, humiliation, relief, confusion and even love for the person who hurt you can all coexist. Trying to skip straight to “positive thinking” often pushes the pain underground, where it lingers.

Some ways to process what you feel:

  • Journal without censoring yourself.
  • Write a letter to the person who cheated that you never send.
  • Cry, punch a pillow, scream into the car on a long drive.
  • Notice when you're ruminating in circles and gently redirect to something absorbing.

Handling intrusive thoughts and triggers

After betrayal, it's very common to replay scenes, imagine details or feel a jolt of panic at a song, a restaurant or a name. These intrusive thoughts aren't a sign that you're weak or obsessed; they're your mind trying to make sense of a shock. A few things that help:

  • Set a “worry window.” Give yourself fifteen minutes a day to think, write or cry about it. When thoughts pop up outside that window, note them and postpone them.
  • Ground yourself. Name five things you can see, four you can hear and three you can touch to bring yourself back to the present.
  • Change the scenery. Rearrange a room, swap out bedding or take a different route to work so daily life holds fewer reminders.

If intrusive thoughts are constant or you can't function day to day, that's an important signal to get professional support.

Talk to a professional

A licensed therapist can be invaluable after infidelity. They can help you manage intrusive thoughts and anxiety, understand your reactions and make decisions from a clearer place. If you're considering staying together, a couples therapist who works with affair recovery can guide you both through honest conversations safely.

Also consider getting a routine sexual health check if there's any chance you've been exposed to an infection. It's a practical step that protects you and can bring peace of mind.

Stay calm before you confront

You'll likely have questions, and you deserve honest answers. But conversations held in the heat of the first shock tend to become shouting matches that leave you with more pain and fewer answers. When you're ready:

  1. Decide what you actually need to know. Some details help you make sense of things; others just replay in your mind.
  2. Choose a private time and place where you won't be interrupted.
  3. Keep it focused on facts and your needs going forward.
  4. Walk away if it turns cruel or circular. You can continue another time.

Deciding whether to stay or leave

Some couples rebuild after infidelity; others shouldn't. Only you can decide, and you don't need to rush. Questions that can help you think it through:

  • Has your partner taken full responsibility without blaming you?
  • Have they ended contact with the other person completely?
  • Are they willing to be transparent and patient while you rebuild trust?
  • Was this a one-time breach, or part of a pattern of dishonesty?
  • Do you still feel love and respect, or mostly obligation and fear?
  • Can you imagine trusting them again with time and effort?

If the answers point toward leaving, you're not giving up — you're choosing yourself. Our guides on how to know when to break up and how to deal with a breakup can help with the next steps.

Rebuilding your self-worth

Infidelity can make you question your attractiveness, your judgment and your value. Rebuilding takes intentional care:

  • Do things that remind you who you are. Return to hobbies, friendships and goals that might have faded during the relationship.
  • Get your body moving. Exercise, dancing, hiking or yoga can help you feel strong and grounded.
  • Try something new. A class, a short trip or a new routine creates fresh experiences that belong only to you.
  • Limit the stalking. Checking the other person's social media keeps the wound open. Mute or block if you need to.
  • Speak to yourself kindly. Notice harsh self-talk and replace it with what you'd tell a friend in the same situation.

Our guide on how to be happy with yourself has more ideas.

Forgiveness — on your timeline

Forgiveness is often misunderstood. It doesn't mean saying what happened was okay, and it doesn't require reconciliation. For many people, forgiveness simply means deciding not to let the betrayal keep controlling their emotions. You may get there in months, years or never — and that's okay. What matters is that you move toward peace in a way that feels true to you, not because someone pressured you.

Learning to trust again

One of the deepest fears after being cheated on is that you'll never trust anyone again. Trust can be rebuilt, slowly. When you're ready to date, take things at a comfortable pace, notice whether words and actions match and remember that caution is healthy, while assuming everyone will betray you is the old wound talking. If trust issues feel overwhelming, working with a therapist can help.

The bottom line

Figuring out how to get over being cheated on isn't about forgetting what happened. It's about grieving honestly, refusing to carry blame that isn't yours, making decisions from a calmer place and rebuilding a life and self-image that feel solid again. Be patient with yourself — healing takes time, and you're allowed to take it. For more support, visit our breakup advice.
takeaways: Being cheated on is not your fault; it was the other person's choice.
In the first days, focus on basics like sleep, food and support — not big decisions.
Let yourself feel the full range of emotions and consider a licensed therapist.
Decide whether to stay or leave based on accountability, transparency and your own needs.
Forgiveness and renewed trust happen on your timeline, not anyone else's.

faq.q: How long does it take to get over being cheated on?
faq.a: There is no fixed timeline. Many people feel the sharpest pain ease over several months, but healing can take longer, especially after a long relationship. Progress often comes in waves, with good days and setbacks. Support from friends and a licensed therapist can make the process feel more manageable.

faq.q: Why do I blame myself for being cheated on?
faq.a: Self-blame can feel like a way to regain control: if it was your fault, you could prevent it next time. But cheating is a choice the other person made instead of communicating or leaving honestly. Relationship problems are shared, but the decision to betray trust is not yours.

faq.q: Can a relationship recover after cheating?
faq.a: Some can, when the person who cheated takes full responsibility, ends contact with the affair partner, stays transparent and is patient while trust is rebuilt. Couples therapy often helps. Recovery is less likely when there is ongoing dishonesty, blame-shifting or a pattern of repeated betrayal.

faq.q: Should I confront the person they cheated with?
faq.a: Usually it brings little relief. The person who owed you honesty and loyalty was your partner. Confronting the other person can escalate drama without giving you useful answers. Focus your energy on your own healing and on the conversations that actually matter for your future.
